title: Leveling the Playing Field -- Ch. 2: Role of the Supreme Court in Economic Development
keywords: Role of the Supreme Court in Economic Development
reclamation of a portion of Manila Bay
primary_topics: Chapter 2 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' -- CJP's address to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas on how the Supreme Court shapes the investment climate, organized into the Court's powers and duties and the jurisprudence that affects investments

An explanation of the Court's five functions -- ordinary review, extraordinary certiorari review for grave abuse, administrative supervision of the lower courts, control of admission to and discipline of the bar, and rule-making including rules protecting constitutional rights

His defense of the Court's most criticized economic rulings: the nullification of the first Oil Deregulation Law in Tatad v. Secretary of Energy because it entrenched a three-company oligopoly, and the voiding of the NAIA Terminal III and Manila Bay reclamation mega contracts, on the principle that an agreement violating the Constitution or the law is not a contract at all

The campaign against the 'CID' plagues of corruption, inefficiency and delay through the Action Program for Judicial Reform, with the disciplinary record to show for it and the support of multilateral agencies and foreign governments

A six-point plea to the business audience -- give suggestions, report victimization, refuse to bribe judges, consult ethical counsel before investing, avoid dubious shortcuts, and read the Court's unnoticed pro-business decisions
sub_topics: He opens with a joke about an investor asking God about a million years and a billion dollars, drawing two lessons: time and money are intertwined, and investments follow timing and returns
He notes what governments want in return -- jobs, national income, infrastructure and other economic benefits -- and states the invitation from the Central Bank and his two-part division of the theme

He describes the Philippine separation of powers, with lawmaking in Congress, implementation in the Presidency and interpretation in the Supreme Court, coequal branches whose coordination underpins economic development

He defines judicial independence concretely: the Court's decisions are final and unreviewable by any other agency, making it the last bulwark of democracy, which requires deciding free of extraneous influence
He contrasts the simpler Philippine structure with countries that split judicial power among constitutional courts, supreme courts and high courts of arbitration
He enumerates the first function, ordinary review of appeals from the Court of Appeals, Sandiganbayan, Court of Tax Appeals and, to a limited extent, the Regional Trial Courts

He explains extraordinary certiorari review and the two ways grave abuse may be committed -- violating the Constitution, laws or settled doctrines, or acting whimsically, arbitrarily or out of bias so as to deny due process

He describes administrative supervision over all lower court judges and personnel, control of the bar examinations, disbarment and the MCLE program, and the rule-making power that lets the Court safeguard the Bill of Rights

He lists the four situations in which the Court's actions move markets and draw business comment: declaring laws or executive orders unconstitutional, invalidating infrastructure mega contracts, issuing injunctions, and disciplining judges
He recounts the backlash to Tatad v. Secretary of Energy, when critics proposed impeaching the justices or amending the Constitution to strip the Court of authority over economic issues

He answers that the law was struck down precisely because it was anti-business, perpetuating the monopoly of Shell, Petron and Caltex and barring new entrants, contrary to the Constitution's mandate of free trade and its disfavor of combinations in restraint of trade
He reports the result: Congress passed a new Oil Deregulation Law without the objectionable provisions, Total, Flying A and Seaoil entered the industry, and the critics eventually praised the Court

He turns to the mega contracts for NAIA Terminal III and the Manila Bay reclamation, and rebuts the sanctity-of-contract objection with the rule that an agreement violating the Constitution or the law is no contract
He illustrates with analogies -- a killer is not immune because he paid for the gun, and a seller of a stolen car cannot collect the price but may be liable for fencing

He reassures investors that the Court has strictly barred trial courts from restraining government infrastructure projects, and discloses that at the Bankers Association's request he was personally tasked to review the rules on restraining orders in foreclosures of nonperforming assets
He defends the preliminary injunction as a shield for the weak against the brute power of police or military and against irreparable injury, a tool of justice and equity that is neutral until misused

He turns to the wider criticism of corruption, inefficiency and delay, the CID plagues he has repeatedly condemned, and to the Action Program for Judicial Reform that pairs discipline of erring judges with better conditions for good ones

He recites the disciplinary record: the first admonition of one of its own members in the Court's 100-year history over the 1999 bar examinations, the dismissal of a Court of Appeals member, the 2002 suspension of the Sandiganbayan presiding justice for delay, and more than 350 lower court judges penalized in three years

He names the reform program's other components and its backers -- the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank, the UNDP, the Asia Foundation, and the governments of Canada, the USA, Japan, the European Union, the Netherlands and Australia
He states the Court's vision of competent, honest and courageous judges delivering quality justice that earns public confidence even when unpalatable to current sentiment

He closes with six requests to his business audience and the assurance that the Court is sensitive to good governance as a prerequisite of lasting growth and will uphold predictable and stable jurisprudence
signature_phrases: When a so-called agreement violates the Constitution or the law, it is not a contract at all.
restraining orders are therefore really tools of justice and equity

these plagues of corruption, inefficiency and delay

stances.claim: An independent Supreme Court whose decisions are final and free of extraneous influence is a prerequisite of a favorable investment climate, because good governance and the rule of law underpin lasting economic growth.
stances.rhetorical_move: institutional exposition addressed to investors: defining independence operationally, then tying it to predictable and stable jurisprudence

stances.claim: The Court struck down the first Oil Deregulation Law not to interfere in business but because the law was itself anti-business, perpetuating the oligopoly of Shell, Petron and Caltex against the Constitution's mandate of free trade.
stances.rhetorical_move: turning the critics' own premise around, then pointing to the outcome -- a genuinely deregulated industry with new entrants and eventual praise from the critics

stances.claim: The sanctity of contracts does not shield the voided mega contracts, because an agreement that violates the Constitution or the law is not a contract at all and cannot claim protection from the very law it ignores.
stances.rhetorical_move: principle stated flatly, then driven home by criminal-law analogies about the purchased gun and the stolen vehicle

stances.claim: Restraining orders and preliminary injunctions are tools of justice and equity meant to protect the weak, including investors, from the brute power of government, and are objectionable only when misused.
stances.rhetorical_move: reframing a business grievance as a safeguard, with the neutrality-of-tools maxim as the hinge

stances.claim: The Court is acting against corruption, inefficiency and delay, as shown by the first admonition of one of its own members in a century, the dismissal of an appellate justice, the suspension of the Sandiganbayan presiding justice and penalties on more than 350 lower court judges in three years.
stances.rhetorical_move: answering a reputational charge with an itemized disciplinary record and a roster of international backers of the reform program

stances.claim: Investors bear their own share of responsibility: they should consult ethical counsel before rather than after committing, comply with bidding requirements, refuse dubious shortcuts, and never agree to bribe judges.
stances.rhetorical_move: direct hortatory appeal in numbered items, with the coma-and-physician analogy for late legal advice

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' reproduced CJP's address to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas on the Supreme Court's role in creating a favorable investment climate. After an opening joke about an investor bargaining with God over a cent, he divided his subject into the Court's powers and duties and the jurisprudence affecting investments. He described the Philippine separation of powers, defined judicial independence as the finality of the Court's decisions and their freedom from extraneous influence, called the Court the last bulwark of democracy, and noted that unlike countries with separate constitutional courts and arbitration tribunals the Philippines vests all judicial power in one tribunal. He enumerated five functions: ordinary review of appeals, extraordinary certiorari review for grave abuse of discretion in its two forms, administrative supervision of all lower courts, control of admission to and discipline of the bar, and rule-making including rules protecting the Bill of Rights. He then took up the rulings that had angered business. The first Oil Deregulation Law, voided in Tatad v. Secretary of Energy, had provoked calls to impeach the justices and to amend the Constitution, yet it was struck down precisely because it was anti-business, perpetuating the monopoly of Shell, Petron and Caltex against the constitutional mandate of free trade; Congress then passed a cleaner law and Total, Flying A and Seaoil entered the market. The voided mega contracts for NAIA Terminal III and the Manila Bay reclamation raised the sanctity-of-contract objection, which he answered with the rule that an agreement violating the Constitution or the law is not a contract at all, illustrated by analogies about a purchased gun and a stolen car. He reassured investors that trial courts are barred from restraining government infrastructure projects, disclosed his own assignment to review the foreclosure injunction rules at the Bankers Association's request, and defended preliminary injunctions as tools of justice and equity. Turning to the plagues of corruption, inefficiency and delay, he described the Action Program for Judicial Reform, the Court's disciplinary firsts and its penalties on more than 350 judges in three years, and the support of the World Bank, the ADB, the UNDP, the Asia Foundation and several foreign governments. He closed with six requests to his audience -- suggestions, reports of victimization, refusal to bribe judges, early legal advice, no dubious shortcuts, and attention to decisions like Tañada v. Angara -- and the assurance that the Court would continue to uphold the rule of law and stable jurisprudence.
